title: Malik al-Mulk
tomorrow: Eli comes to apologize. how do you take it without shrinking him?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ar-Ra'uf, the Most Kind, read two ways: mercy turned all the way up, or mercy that lifts a weight. The line: tender. Now, a question about who owns what.

Keys. A house key, a car fob, a little one for a bike lock or a locker. A keyring is a short list of everything we call mine. Yesterday's question came from a thirteen-year-old with a spray can, who said a wall belongs to whoever paints it. That's wrong. But it's a crooked version of a real question, one the Qur'an asks out loud: whose is anything, really?
screen: `A KEYRING: WHAT WE CALL MINE.` → `WHOEVER PAINTS IT?` → `WHOSE IS ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: Today's Name is Malik al-Mulk, Owner of All Sovereignty. Mulk is having in every size: a throne, a kingdom, a corner store, a set of keys. Here's the verse, in Pickthall's words: "Say: O Allah! Owner of Sovereignty! Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt. Thou exaltest whom Thou wilt, and Thou abasest whom Thou wilt. In Thy hand is the good. Lo! Thou art Able to do all things." Notice the first word, Qul, say. This verse is written to be spoken. So, the wall. It isn't the painter's. And in the deepest sense it isn't fully the owner's either: what anyone holds is given, and can be withdrawn. That doesn't make the wall fair game. It makes the owner a caretaker, holding something on loan, and a borrowed thing gets more care, not less. And here's a detail to tell a friend tonight. The verse lists giving and taking, raising and lowering. Then it says only: in Thy hand is the good. Some commentators notice that it names the good alone, and read that as courtesy in how we speak to God.
screen: `OWNER OF SOVEREIGNTY.` · `GIVEN, AND WITHDRAWN.` · `NOT FAIR GAME: ON LOAN.` · `IN THY HAND IS THE GOOD.` · then, large: `OWNER OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Take your keys, or any small thing you'd call yours, and rest it in an open palm. Say the verse's first and last lines aloud, slowly: O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, and, in Thy hand is the good. Then leave your hand open, the thing resting there and not gripped, for the rest of the sit.
screen: `KEYS IN AN OPEN PALM.` · `O ALLAH! OWNER OF SOVEREIGNTY!` · `IN THY HAND IS THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Malik al-Mulk. Owner of All Sovereignty: the One who gives every kind of having, and takes it back.
Carry this: owner of all, and everything on your keyring held on loan, with care. Fifteen fifty-eight, done.

chat.says: dad says the wall isn't really 'ours,' it's 'on loan.' so Eli was RIGHT?? i'm so confused
options: No. On loan means your dad cares for it more, not that anyone can grab it.
Yes. If nothing is truly ours, a wall is fair game for any painter.
No. It's your dad's fully, forever; God owning it is only a figure of speech.
chat.meaning: Malik al-Mulk gives and withdraws every kind of having. What we hold is on loan, which makes us caretakers, not anyone's free canvas.
